sentences.text: The order dated 07.04.2021 in W.P.No.206413/2016 has given rise to these three writ appeals.
W.A.No.200170/2021 is filed by the legal representatives of the writ petitioner namely Muralidhar Rao.
W.A.No.200100/2021 is filed by respondents 8 to 11 in the writ petition.
W.A.No.200127/2021 is filed by legal representative no.7 (II) of the seventh respondent in the writ petition namely Sri Shivabasappa.
2. For the sake of convenience, the parties are referred with respect to position of each of them in the writ petition.
The material facts are as follows.
3. The writ petitioner was the owner of 15 acres 36 guntas of land in Sy.No.3 and 12 acres 14 guntas in Sy.No.4 of Kotnoor village, Gulbarga taluk and district.
The seventh respondent's father owned 13 acres 9 guntas in Sy.No.5 and 4 acres 34 guntas in Sy.No.2 of the same village.

On 01.12.1958, the Government of Mysore issued a notification to acquire land to an extent of 28 acres 10 guntas in Sy.No.3 for the purpose of establishing Seed Multiplication Farm and Agricultural School.
Pursuant to the notification, the Government passed an award.
Then in the year guntas in Sy.No.2 were acquired, and compensation was paid to the seventh respondent in respect of acquisition of land in Sy.No.5.

He did not receive compensation in relation to acquisition of land in Sy.No.2.
4.
It appears that the Government did not utilize 4 acres 10 guntas of land in Sy.No.3 that belonged to the writ petitioner.

Then the seventh respondent made an application to the Government on 07.05.1979 requesting to return the said land or to grant it to him as he had become land less after the acquisition of all his lands.

Considering this requisition, the sixth respondent i.e., the Deputy Commissioner, Kalaburagi issued a notice to the seventh respondent on 13.03.1995 directing him to make payment of Rs.96,509/- which was the market value of the land to an extent of 4 acres 10 guntas in Sy.No.3.
He was asked to make this payment within fifteen days.
The writ petitioner stated that this order of the Government was contrary to its earlier order to the effect that the land should be returned to the original owner.

Then, the seventh respondent appears to have questioned the demand made by the Government for money by filing a writ petition in W.P.No.15653/1995 which came to be dismissed on 06.06.1995 holding that the seventh respondent was not entitled to seek exchange of land.

Subsequently, seventh respondent died and his son again gave representations dated 25.06.1998 and 31.08.2000 to the sixth respondent requesting to grant the land to him as he was ready and willing to pay the market value of the land.

His representations were accepted and the Government granted the land to him i.e., 4 acres 10 guntas in Sy.No.3 in accordance with Rule 7 of Karnataka Land Grant Rules, 1969 by receiving the market value on 11.12.2006.
This order of re-grant in favour of the seventh respondent was called in question in the writ petition.

5. The learned Single Judge, disposed of the writ petition by passing the following order:
Shri Shivabasappa S/O Sidramappa ... vs The State Of Karnataka And Ors on 13 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31433229/
7

"(1) The order dated 29-01-2007, Annexure-A to the writ petition is quashed and the matter is remitted back to respondents 1 and 2/State to re-examine the entire issue of whether - (a) The compensation was received by both the petitioner and the 7th respondent on acquisition of their respective lands?
(b) The Government order dated 28- 07-1993 directing return of the land to the original owner is to be acted upon?
(c) The land was granted to the 7th respondent on an application after the death of the father of the 7th respondent alleged to have been signed by the father of the 7th respondent?
and hold a detailed inquiry, hear both the petitioner and the 7th respondent, examine the record in its entirety and then pass appropriate orders in accordance with law.
(2) The aforesaid exercise shall be concluded by the State Government within 6 months from the date of receipt of copy of this order.

(3) No costs."
6.
We have heard the arguments of learned Senior Counsel Sri S.M. Chandrashekhar and Sri Ashok Haranahalli, and Sri R.S. Sidhapurkar and Sri Mallikarjun C. Basareddy, learned Government Advocate.

7. The impugned order shows that the learned Single Judge has traced the undisputed facts in five steps and arrived at an opinion that the order of granting the land to seventh respondent in the teeth of Government order dated 28.07.1993 directing the re-grant of land in favour of the original owner is erroneous.
The father of the seventh respondent chose not to proceed further during his life time after the dismissal of his writ petition.
His father died on 31.08.2000.
Four years after the death, the seventh respondent made a representation putting his father's signature.

Even in the subsequent representation dated 26.08.2004, the seventh respondent narrated the fact that he had a given a representation on 31.01.2008 which is contrary to the record and therefore the proceeding in relation to grant of land in favour of seventh respondent by the Government was based on an application which appears to be forged and thus the proceeding rendered itself erroneous.

It is further observed by the learned Single Judge that the sale of land by the seventh respondent immediately after he took over its possession ran counter to the representations made by his father that he required the land for cultivation as he became landless after the acquisition of his entire land.
This transaction would clearly show that the seventh respondent wanted the land for trade or commerce and not for cultivation.
In this view, the matter requires to be decided by the Government once again.
Giving these reasons the learned Single Judge passed the order as extracted above.

8 8.

S.M. Chandrashekhar appearing for Sri R.J. Bhusare, learned counsel for the appellants in W.A.No.200170/2021, argued that the learned Single Judge grossly erred in remanding the case to the Government for consideration.
It was the decision of the Government to return 4.10 acres of land to the appellant's father, and if this was the clear decision, there was no necessity to remand.
The writ petition ought to have been allowed quashing the order of granting land to the seventh respondent.

He argued further that the seventh respondent's father was not the owner of any extent of land in Sy.No.3, the decision to grant the land to the seventh respondent was contrary to its earlier decision that 4.10 acres of land in Sy.No.3 should be returned to its original owner.
For this reason, the seventh respondent's father could not have laid claim for grant of land, and in fact he did not pursue the matter once he was asked to make payment of Rs.96,509/-.
Actually seventh respondent is not interested in land, and the persons behind him are purchasers from him.
This becomes evident from the challan at Annexure-P which shows that a sum of Rs.6,37,500/- was actually paid by Sri S.H. Jadhav, a purchaser from the seventh respondent even before the grant.
After grant of land in favour of seventh respondent, he sold away the land within a few days.
All these transactions are not disputed, but they clearly show that seventh respondent did not want the land and the purchasers behind him are the interested persons.

Seventh respondent was not a landless person and he played fraud on the Government in obtaining the grant of land in his favour,
he argued.

9. It was the further argument of Sri S.M. Chandrashkehar that according to Section 101 of Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act,
2013, if any land which was acquired remains unutilized for a period of five years from the date of taking over possession, it should be returned to the original owner or his heirs.

Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act,
2013
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Even though in the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, such a provision was not there, the policy was to return the land to the person from whom land was acquired.
For this reason the petitioners became entitled to claim return of land to them.

10. In regard to delay on the part of the petitioners, Sri S.M. Chandrashekhar submitted that the petitioners were not the aware of all the developments as the order of grant of land to the seventh respondent had not been communicated to them.

Only when they saw some activities in the land,
they enquired and came to know everything that had taken place behind their back.

As the petitioners are the original owners, and the Government order also is to the effect that the land should be returned to the original owners, mere delay should not defeat their legitimate claim and therefore he argued for allowing the writ appeal filed by the petitioners.
11. Sri Ashok Haranahalli, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondents argued that the writ petitioners were not the aggrieved parties as they did not seek allotment of land to them.
Nine years after the grant was made in favour of seventh respondent, they filed the writ petition which was devoid of merits.
In fact, the petitioners were aware that the seventh respondent's father first made an application seeking grant of land and also about the representation given by the seventh respondent.
They never made any application.
In this view, they had no right to file writ petition.
12. It was the further argument of Sri Ashok Haranahalli that once the land was acquired according to due process of law and compensation was paid to the land losers, the latter do not get any right.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 9 The acquiring authority has got every right to utilize the land for any purpose and it can grant the land to anybody.
For this reason, the grant made in favour of seventh respondent is not illegal.
13. His further point of argument was that after the grant was made, third party interest was created.
The sale made by the respondent No.7 in favour of respondent Nos.8 to 11 cannot be said to be illegal as they are the purchasers for valuable consideration.
Actually the grant in favour of seventh respondent was for an upset price equal to market value and therefore he had every right to deal with the land in any way he liked.
He further argued that this being the position, the learned Single Judge ought not to have remanded the case to the Government for taking a re-decision.
Therefore the impugned order requires to be set aside and consequently the writ petition should be dismissed.
Sri Ashok Haranahalli has placed reliance on some decisions to which we refer later.
14. We have considered the arguments.

15. The question emanating for discussion is whether the learned Single Judge was right in remanding the case to the first respondent to examine three points mentioned in the operative portion of the impugned order.
16. What we notice is after acquisition of the lands belonging to the petitioners, they received the compensation.

Though Sri S.M. Chandrashekhar argued that the petitioners did not receive compensation, his argument is contrary to the petitioners' pleading in the writ petition; in para 3 of the writ petition they have clearly stated that award was passed and they received the compensation.
Likewise, it was the argument of counsel for the seventh respondent that the father of the seventh respondent did not receive compensation after acquisition of his land in Sy.No.2.

From the facts pleaded in the writ petition, it may be inferred that the petitioners were not interested in getting back the piece of land i.e., 4.10 acres in Sy.No.3, which remained unutilized by the Government, and they did not give any representation to the Government claiming grant of that land.
The father of the seventh respondent first gave a representation to the Government on 07.05.1979 seeking grant of land.
The decision of the Government was that the land should be returned to its original owner.
Sofar as land in Sy.No.3 is concerned, the original owner was the writ petitioner, not the father of the seventh respondent.

Despite the fact that the Government ordered for return of land to the original owner, the Deputy Commissioner directed the father of seventh respondent to make payment of Rs.96,509/- for the grant of land to him, and it appears he lost interest over the land after he failed in his writ petition 15653/1995.
And he died in the year 1996 as is evident from the death certificate produced at Annexure-H.

Even though in the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, such a provision was not there, the policy was to return the land to the person from whom land was acquired.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
The legal position as to State acquiring absolute right over land vested in it after acquisition in accordance with law, and its power to put the unutilized land for a different purpose is settled.
And there is no impediment as such for a land loser to seek grant of unutilized land.
Section 101 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013, now provides for returning such land.
If they did not seek grant of land, did they have right to challenge the order of grant in favour of seventh respondent being interested persons, is the question that obviously arises in the backdrop of entire scenario and the decisions of the Supreme Court in the cases of AYAAUBKHAN NOORKHAN PATHAN vs STATE OF MAHARASHTRA AND OTHERS [(2013) 4 SCC 465];

23. If the seventh respondent has committed fraud in getting the land granted to him, it should not be sustained.
Before that, as discussed above, the Government has to examine what it meant when it said that the land should be granted or returned to original owner relating to Sy.No.3.
If the land grabbers are behind the parties, we do not hesitate in saying that the Government land must be protected from them and the Government can utilize the land for any other public purpose.
opennyai_summary.decision:
The Government can reconsider the order of grant made in favour of seventh respondent.
The land can also be kept in Land Bank.
All these aspects are to be thrashed out judiciously.
Therefore we do not find any infirmity in the impugned order which has directed remand.
